summary: Defines an option that lets two ends of a PPP link negotiate IPv6 datagram compression through the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP). It replaces RFC 2472's treatment of this option. PPP is a method for carrying network-layer traffic across point-to-point links. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people on a phone line agree to use shorthand to talk faster. This paper defines the way two computers agree to use shortened IPv6 messages over a direct link.

questions: how does ppp negotiate ipv6 compression
what is the ipv6 compression protocol option
subtitle: How the two ends of a PPP link agree to compress IPv6 packets, using one option in the IPv6 Control Protocol.

tldr.problem: Two ends of a point-to-point link may want to shrink IPv6 packets with a header compression method, but they need a standard way to agree on which one.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv6-Compression-Protocol option (type 2) in IPV6CP carries a two-octet value naming the compression protocol, plus optional data for that protocol. Each end requests it for the direction it wants to receive.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5172 obsoletes RFC 2472 together with RFC 5072 and, according to the text, introduces no protocol changes over RFC 2472.

today: RFC 5172 is a Proposed Standard and, per the unit metadata, no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2472 (together with RFC 5072), and the text states that no protocol changes were introduced over RFC 2472.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) has three main parts: a method for encapsulating datagrams over serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring network-layer protocols.

RFC 5172 defines one parameter for the NCP used by IPv6, the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP): the compression parameter for IPv6 datagram compression. The Interface Identifier parameter lives in the companion document, RFC 5072.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two computers on a cable can talk, they first agree on the rules, a bit like two friends agreeing on a game before they play. This paper adds one rule: whether to use shorthand.

sections.title: Where IPV6CP Fits in a PPP Link
sections.content:
To set up a link, each end first sends LCP packets to configure and test the data link. After that, PPP sends NCP packets to choose and configure one or more network-layer protocols. Once a network-layer protocol is configured, its datagrams can flow over the link.

The link stays configured until explicit LCP or NCP packets close it, or until some external event occurs, such as a power failure at the other end or a carrier drop. IPV6CP is the NCP that does this configuration for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two ends shake hands to make the link work. Then they talk about the details of each kind of traffic. IPV6CP is the talk about IPv6 traffic.

sections.title: The IPv6-Compression-Protocol Option
sections.content:
IPV6CP uses the same Configuration Option format as LCP, but with its own set of options. If an option is left out of a Configure-Request, its default value is assumed. The only option defined here is IPv6-Compression-Protocol, Type 2.

The option signals the ability to receive compressed packets. Each end MUST request it separately if compression is wanted in both directions. By default, compression is not enabled.

The option is specific to IPv6 datagrams. It is not to be confused with compression negotiated through the PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP), which can affect all datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side says which shorthand it can understand when listening. If you want shorthand both ways, both sides have to ask for it. If nobody asks, everyone speaks normally.

sections.title: Option Format and Field Values
sections.content:
The option has a Type of 2, a Length of at least 4, a two-octet IPv6-Compression-Protocol field, and a Data field of zero or more octets whose content depends on the chosen compression protocol.

The two-octet value is always the same as the PPP Data Link Layer Protocol field value for that compression protocol. Values have been assigned for IP Header Compression (0061) and for Robust Header Compression (ROHC) (0003). Other assignments can be made in documents that define specific compression algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small label with a number on it that says which shorthand you mean, plus room for extra notes that only that shorthand understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without proper link security such as authentication before data transfer, man-in-the-middle attacks could cost data integrity and confidentiality. The RFC lists three appropriate mechanisms: access control lists that filter traffic received over the link, an authentication protocol that lets peers pick an authentication method such as MD5, and an encryption control protocol for choosing encryption algorithms.

Even with these in place, threats remain. For example, MD5 authentication exposes a link to replay attacks. Readers are pointed to RFC 3748 for a generic threat model.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure you know who is on the other end of the line before you start talking, and use a secret code if the conversation is private.

sections.title: IANA and Management Considerations
sections.content:
No new assignment is needed. Option type 2 is already in the "PPP IPV6CP CONFIGURATION OPTIONS" registry, and only its RFC reference changed to 5172. The compression protocol values are the same as PPP protocol field values, so future allocation follows RFC 3818, which requires IETF Consensus. The "IPv6-Compression-Protocol Types" registry reference likewise changed to 5172.

For management, the status of the negotiation and the compression algorithm on the link should be observable by an operator, but the RFC says no standard management interface covers this at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers already had this option in it, so only the name of the paper that describes it was updated. Nobody has yet made a standard way to check which shorthand a link is using.

fields.name: IPv6-Compression-Protocol
fields.desc: The compression protocol wanted; same as its PPP protocol field value.
